strengths: Addresses a real and important problem: automated security benchmark generation to overcome contamination, extensibility, and difficulty scaling issues
Solid methodology with well-designed pipeline featuring multiple validation loops, execution-driven refinement, and plausibility checks at each stage

Comprehensive evaluation including validation against human-written BAXBENCH tests (81.6% precision/recall on functional tests), systematic expert evaluation with inter-rater agreement metrics, and honest documentation of failure modes
Practical value through public release of 40 new scenarios with three difficulty levels; cost-effective (~$4/scenario) compared to ~3 hours of expert time
Thorough experimental setup with detailed prompts, algorithms, ablation studies on model choice, and clear reproducibility information
Excellent presentation with clear pipeline explanation, illuminating SVGBadge case study, and comprehensive appendices documenting limitations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applies well-established LLM techniques (execution feedback, iterative refinement, self-correction) to a new application domain rather than introducing methodological innovations

Significant reliability concerns: 17 CWE-400 exploits acknowledged as spurious with arbitrary cutoffs; forced to exclude CWE-400 from main evaluation; expert evaluation shows 96.77% soundness score with 3.23% potential improvement margin

Coverage gaps: only 71% of exploits rated for 'high coverage' by experts; documented failure modes show false positives (Login scenario), false negatives (FrameExtract scenario), and functional test bugs (OpenAPI misinterpretation)
Narrow scope limiting generalizability: only REST API web backends, only BAXBENCH-scope CWEs (11 types), unclear scaling to other programming paradigms or vulnerability classes

Model contamination and evaluation limitations: had to exclude evaluation of generating models (GPT-5, CLAUDE-4, DEEPSEEK-R1) to avoid bias; ablation shows 14.4% performance difference (95.2% vs 80.8%) between self-generated and cross-generated benchmarks; expert evaluation only on 6 of 40 new scenarios

Presentation issues: important limitations (CWE-400, failure modes) relegated to appendix; overstated claims about 'outmatching' BAXBENCH when 33% false positives in security tests; incremental benchmark contribution (40 new scenarios) limits novelty

strengths: Addresses important, timely problem of sustainable code security benchmark generation with clear motivation regarding contamination and scalability
Methodologically sound three-stage pipeline with elegant design (iterative refinement, flag system for exploit validation, reference solutions)

Rigorous validation including quantitative comparison with BAXBENCH (83.5% functional agreement), manual expert verification, systematic expert evaluation with 4 reviewers, and comprehensive ablations
Practical impact: generated 40 novel scenarios at 12× speedup compared to manual creation, costing <$10/task, with public release
Commendable transparency about limitations with detailed analysis of failure modes (CWE-400 issues, coverage concerns, generation bias) and honest exclusion of problematic tests
Comprehensive experimental design across 8 models from 6 providers with attention to contamination and bias concerns
Well-executed end-to-end system with clear prompts, case studies, and reproducible released benchmark
weaknesses: CWE-400 (resource exhaustion) exploits highly problematic: ~17% of generated exploits involve CWE-400; expert evaluation shows ALL 4 sampled CWE-400 tests raise concerns; fix is exclusion not resolution, suggesting fundamental pipeline limitations

Exploit generalization concerns: expert evaluation reports 71% average coverage with low inter-rater agreement (22.58%); 67% of non-CWE-400 exploits have false negative concerns per at least one reviewer; experts note exploits may not generalize to new implementations

Generation bias inadequately addressed: CLAUDE-4.5 achieves 45.2% sec_pass@1 on self-generated vs. 35.5% on GPT-5-generated benchmarks (9.7pp advantage); pass@1 shows similar bias (95.2% vs. 80.8%); ablation limited to only 3-4 scenarios
Limited scope reduces applicability: restricted to REST API backends only; covers only 11 of hundreds of CWEs; limited to specific programming languages/frameworks

Insufficient scenario diversity validation: novelty ensured through rejection sampling on titles only; no quantitative diversity metrics or semantic similarity analysis; claims of novelty lack empirical support

Failure modes not fully resolved: FrameExtract scenario shows exploit overfitting to specific endpoints causing false negatives; Login scenario exhibits functional unsoundness from OpenAPI ambiguity; suggests pipeline perpetuates errors
Reference solution dependency unclear: test/exploit quality may depend on using only 4 specific LLMs for reference solutions; no analysis of sensitivity to solution LLM choice
Limited ground truth comparison: primarily validated against BAXBENCH (also automated); no comparison with actual vulnerability databases; expert evaluation covers only 12 of 40 scenarios
Technical choices not justified: maximum 5 refinement iterations appears arbitrary; no sensitivity analysis; temperature/sampling choices (0.4) lack justification

strengths: Addresses practical problem of expensive benchmark creation with 12× effort reduction
Rigorous validation against BAXBENCH with 80.9% agreement on functional tests and 98.6% exploit soundness
Well-engineered three-phase pipeline with principled iterative refinement using execution feedback
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 14 models with multiple ablation studies and contamination analysis
Honest about limitations including false negatives, false positives, and inter-rater disagreement; discovers BAXBENCH errors
Clever technical design: contrastive solution generation, FLAG system for exploit refinement, appropriate guardrails
Will be released publicly enabling future research on automated benchmark generation
weaknesses: Remaining quality concerns: only 71% exploit coverage rated high (Table 7); 164 false negatives vs. BAXBENCH; low inter-rater agreement (22.58%)
Domain-specific failures unresolved: CWE-400 exploits often spurious; CWE-522 largely missed; some exploits overfit to reference solutions
Limited technical novelty: iterative refinement with execution feedback is standard; no insights into why security test generation succeeds or fails
Narrow scope restricted to REST API backends and BAXBENCH CWEs; not generalizable to other domains or vulnerability classes
Benchmark difficulty doesn't substantially challenge models: 83% pass@1 on HARD split; model rankings similar to BAXBENCH
Reproducibility limited by proprietary model dependence (GPT-5, Claude-4.5); design choices lack justification; only 12 scenarios manually verified
Paper length (48 pages) with substantial content in appendices; Algorithm pseudo-code dense; limited discussion of failure modes in main narrative

strengths: Addresses an important and practical bottleneck in security benchmarking by automating the creation of scenarios, functional tests, and security exploits, reducing human effort by 12x
Well-designed three-step pipeline with clever technical choices (flag system for REFINEEXPLOIT, contrastive solution approach, iterative refinement using execution feedback)

Comprehensive validation including quantitative comparison with BAXBENCH (80.9% agreement on functional tests), manual audit of 71 exploits (98.6% soundness), and expert evaluation across 12 scenarios
Strong contamination controls with calibrated bias analysis and ablation studies showing Spearman rank correlation >0.9 across disjoint model sets, addressing concerns about benchmark integrity
Significant practical impact with clear cost-benefit (tasks generated in <2 hours for <$4) and three difficulty levels enabling capability-matched evaluation
Thorough presentation with detailed appendices, comprehensive prompts, algorithms, real case studies (SVGBadge), and honest failure mode analysis
Enables continuous benchmark generation addressing training data contamination risks, supporting future evaluation of advancing LLM capabilities
Strong reproducibility commitment with public release of methods, code, and AUTOBAXBENCH dataset
weaknesses: Limited scope restricted to REST API web backends; generalizability to ABIs, CLI interfaces, and other domains remains unexplored despite being listed as future work

Reliability issues with specific CWE types: CWE-400 (resource exhaustion) generates spurious exploits and is excluded rather than addressed; CWE-522 (plaintext credentials) exhibits 73% false negative rate due to LLMs not naturally exploring database inspection

Minimal human audit coverage of new benchmark: only 6 of 40 AUTOBAXBENCH scenarios manually verified, with 71% average coverage rating and low inter-rater agreement (22.58% on exploit coverage assessment)

Elevated false negative/positive rates: 7.4% miss rate vs BAXBENCH; exploits demonstrate overfitting to reference solutions (FrameExtract unspecified /uploads endpoint) or excessive permissiveness (Login accepting multiple status codes)
Arbitrary design parameters without principled justification: maximum 5 refinement iterations based on observation rather than analysis; no sensitivity studies
Heavy dependency on expensive frontier models (GPT-5, Claude 4.5 Sonnet); cost analysis excludes orchestration LLM API calls; generalization to open-weight models insufficiently explored
Potential confirmation bias in exploit verification: same LLM generating exploit strategies also verifies compliance; no independent correctness validation mechanism
Limited root-cause analysis of vulnerability-type difficulty: paper identifies CWE-400/CWE-522 as hard but provides no deeper investigation into why or proposed solutions beyond exclusion

Comparison with BAXBENCH not entirely fair: AUTOBAXBUILDER generates more comprehensive exploits by design (iterates over multiple solutions), making 'reproduced or outmatched' claims somewhat tautological
Potential long-term contamination risk: AUTOBAXBENCH will enter training data of future LLMs, creating feedback loops that could degrade benchmark utility over time
